title: My plans. My ambition
writing:
**“The quest for a better life has been an unending aspiration of the human civilization and will remain so till the end of time—that is if time ever ends”—Babatunde Raji Fashola (BRF)**

I created this website for 2 reasons. First to serve as a blueprint for my plans and ambitions—so I can always be reminded of what line of action is next. And second, to have personal conversations with myself on topics I do not see enough people talking about—topics like how do we bring about prosperity, and fixing things in our country that are obviously not working.

Nigeria is a complex place. There is never just one obstacle people with brilliant ideas like myself have to overcome. There are many problems like how do you access capital to fund your business; how do you succeed in a country with no infrastructural support from the government; how do you establish a sustainable business in a country where the people keep getting poor; or where the literacy level is low; or where the quality of the workforce, businesses, government agencies are terrible.

Considering these obstacles, I’ve struggled with deciding where to start.

After a lot of thinking and reading books on the development of the civilization of other countries, I have decided there are 4 critical industries to develop Nigeria, and they are; **software, energy, industrialization, and infrastructure.**

## Software

I decided the best industry to start with is computer science—learning and accumulating as much knowledge as I can on creating useful and impactful software products.

My reason for this is simple. I believe software development is one of the few industries that demands the least resources to get started—relative to other industries—but can also have a huge and pervasive impact.

Despite my country’s complexities, there are certain factors we enjoy with the rest of the world that makes software the right starting point. First is the low barrier to entry to creating software; with the advent of AI and free online resources, learning how to code has never been easier. Second is the ubiquity of smartphones which means the potential users of your software is unimaginable—depending on its usefulness. And the last is impact—great software products easily travel the world faster than physical products restrained by geography.

My ultimate goal is to build a company and products that serve as the critical backbone of the country’s software infrastructure that every other enterprise and products rely on. The money made from software should then be invested in the next critical industry—energy.

## Energy

“Energy is the master resource; it’s how we feed ourselves, build shelter, and make everything we need to live comfortably” —Peter Thiel

The reason energy is so important is because it powers everything we do; it enables us to run our business, transport ourselves from point A to B, charge our phones and laptops, and even cook. Energy is literally at the foundation of everything we do. This is why we need to get it right.

Energy comes in different forms that can be generated from different natural resources some of which Nigeria is lucky to possess like crude oil and natural gas. So what’s the excuse for our dilapidated energy? Well, I believe it’s a combination of mismanagement and lack of indigenous engineering talent to effectively produce and distribute what we need.

I agree corruption is a problem in Nigeria’s energy sector, but I believe this fixation on corruption distracts us from a more profound problem facing our energy sector which is the lack of capable indigenous engineering talent to use our natural resources to generate the energy we need. Proof of this is the fact that Nigeria’s export is dominated by raw materials like crude oil, natural gas, and agricultural raw materials, which are then imported back into Nigeria as finished goods produced in other countries.

I believe it is our inability to turn our natural resources into finished goods ourselves that encourages corruption. When we get the indigenous talent to accomplish this ourselves, better and reliable energy will be equitably distributed across Nigeria regardless of how much corruption is going on.

If we don’t succeed or get this right then the next 2 industries will be 10x more difficult to succeed in. When we succeed in generating reliable and cheaper energy ourselves, we move to the next industry—industrialization.

## Industrialization

Industrialization is when society stops relying on manual labor and small-scale production, and shifts to machines, factories, and large-scale systems to mass produce. This means machines replacing humans where necessary, building factories, and increase in infrastructure like railways, energy, and logistics to make industrial operations easier.

A degree of industrialization exists in Nigeria; the current state of industrialization comprises local and multinational industries mass producing their goods. My experience working in a factory located in an industrial environment gave me two remarkable insights into the industry; first is that our local industries are not globally competitive because of the quality of their operations, and second is the incompetence of the Nigerian workforce.

I worked in an aluminum company located in a local government area called Ado-Odo Ota in Ogun State. The factory I worked in was specifically located in a town called Igbesa and it comprises many factories. The industries actually extend beyond Ado-Odo Ota and include another town called Agbara that also has many factories but mostly multinational ones.

I worked 7AM to 7PM from Monday to Saturday, meaning Sunday was the only free time I had. I often took walks around and sometimes a bus to Agbara to see how things are over there. The first problem our local industries face is the lack of infrastructural support from the government, the second is our local industries being stuck in a 19th-century-like American industrialization where all they care about is maximizing profit at the expense of their workers, and the third problem is the lack of a competent Nigerian workforce.

Unlike the software and energy sector, we don’t need to and can’t even reinvent the wheel when it comes to Nigeria’s industrialization. We can only improve it by making things better. These problems are the reasons our local industries can’t manufacture globally competitive goods, and if we are going to get the full benefit of industrialization we need to start exporting globally competitive made-in-Nigeria products.

## Infrastructure

“Human felicity is produced not so much by great pieces of good fortune that seldom happen, as by little advantages that occur every day” —Benjamin Franklin

Simply put, infrastructure is the systems and structures we build to make everyday life smoother, safer, and less stressful. Therefore, this isn’t a mission that will be left till the end after succeeding in software, energy, and industrialization. Instead, it will be executed simultaneously.

This means doing things as simple as building better and cleaner roads, clean water systems, hospitals and clinics, public campaigns and initiatives to increase literacy, building better markets, security, and so on. Better infrastructure is the easiest to accomplish, and when we get this right we will see an increase in the quality of life of our people.

## Is This too Much to Accomplish in One Lifetime?

“Because a thing is difficult for you, do not therefore suppose it to be beyond mortal power. On the contrary, if anything is possible and proper for man to do, assume it must fall within your own capacity”—Marcus Aurelius

When I was about finishing this writing, a question I asked myself is “isn’t this too much for one person to attempt to accomplish in one lifetime?”

Well, I think it is. At the same time, I don’t think it is impossible. So, In Sha Allah, I will see it to the end.

Like Lasuites say; Ahead Ahead.

title: The Bad News is that Nothing in Nigeria Works. The Good News is that this Means there is a lot to Build
writing:
## The bad news

I have come to the conclusion that nothing in Nigeria works. I mean this literally; nothing in the country functions as it is supposed to.

Starting with our education system, our schools—from primary to tertiary—do a terrible job of teaching and preparing Nigerians for the real world. The outdated curriculum, uncomfortable school buildings, and poor teacher welfare all lead to our educational system producing graduates that are incapable of solving real-world problems.

Then there is the issue of unemployment and underemployment. The thousands of graduates produced every year are unable to secure befitting jobs, partly due to a massive skills gap and partly due to the country’s high unemployment rate. The few graduates who put in the work to upskill themselves are often unable to secure well-paying jobs, so they end up underemployed or, worse, leaving the country.

Then there is the problem with our roads, housing, and infrastructure. Our roads are bad, littered with trash, and filled with potholes. In places where they are worse, they cost Nigerians their lives. The houses we live in are uninspiring, often built for survival rather than comfort. The little infrastructure we do have is falling apart due to old age and poor maintenance; our railroads and airports are prime examples. Our internet and digital tools, like online payment systems, are unreliable, and our public transportation is deeply uncomfortable.

There is also the problem of insecurity and lawlessness. Boko Haram has been causing havoc for over 10 years in the North, and traveling interstate is terrifying because there is a probability of getting kidnapped or even killed by "unknown gunmen" you did not provoke. Even civil violations are difficult to resolve because you need to be financially buoyant to navigate the police and the courts.

To the energy problem: Our electricity in literally every part of the country still goes on and off, costing us millions of naira in business and productivity. The price of petrol is volatile, making transportation expensive. Those who can afford gas cookers lament every time they go to refill their cylinders because the price per kilogram has increased, and even the most vulnerable, still using kerosene stoves, are not spared.

Then to our health sector. First, the doctors, nurses, and healthcare personnel are treated terribly, with no regard or respect for the sanctity of their profession. Then there is the inaccessibility of hospitals and pharmacies due to how expensive healthcare services and medicines have become.

How about starting a business? How convenient is that? First, access to capital and loans is not inclusive and is mostly reserved for the "big men" who are already wealthy. Starting a business—whether formally or informally—is difficult because you have to jump through hoops. You also have to factor in a lot of other considerations, like how to make the business sustainable when people keep getting poorer due to inflation. And if you need it, access to reliable data on different segments of the country is virtually non-existent, so you have to rely on guesswork.

Finally, the funniest part is that being a wealthy Nigerian doesn’t save you from these problems. No matter how much money you have, your children still have to go through the terrible education system, so you send them abroad. You still have to drive on the same pothole-riddled roads and sit in traffic for long hours in your fancy cars. You still have to worry about insecurity when traveling interstate because killers and kidnappers don’t discriminate. You still have to worry about the quality of our healthcare sector, so you seek services abroad. You also live in uninspiring environments with terrible sewage systems and trash-littered roads leading up to your gate. You also have to jump through hoops just to start a business, so you bribe your way through. And the most embarrassing part: your house also goes pitch black when "NEPA" takes the light unexpectedly. But it’s fine, because you own a generator.

The truth is, there is no problem the poor and middle-class Nigerians face that the rich doesn’t. The difference is the latter has the money to spend to solve these problems for the time being. Which wouldn’t be necessary if things just worked.

## The good news

The silver lining here is that there is a lot to build. There is so much work to be done that it excites me, and I believe the earlier we start, the earlier we can shape Nigeria into what we want it to be.

title: Nigerian Public Discourse by Babatunde Raji Fashola (BRF)
writing:
I regard this book as one of the most important books for Nigeria. I see it as a kind of holy book—pointing the way so we can make Nigeria what we want her to be.

It’s easy to disregard it because of its size and dismiss it as just another piece of text on the history and problems of Nigeria. But after reading it several times, I’ve come to realize that what it does is concisely explain how the Nigerian political system works, while also calling on us Nigerians to roll up our sleeves and contribute to the building of our country—which is the most important part.

The book made me realize that maybe Nigeria is not as bad as we think. Maybe the negative images we have of our country are exaggerated. That we, the citizens, are doing more harm than good by dragging her name through the mud. At the same time, the book doesn’t deny that we have a lot to fix.

Most importantly, it lets us know there is hope for redemption—and that with the right mindset, intelligence, and strategies, we can make her the prosperous nation we want her to be.

Matters like corruption and other problems plaguing our country are mentioned in the book. It would be very dishonest to turn a blind eye to these issues while clamouring for patriotism. But I chose to focus on the most important part: to stop humiliating our country and, more importantly, to roll up our sleeves and build her.

In the book, BRF talks about “the quest for a better life as an unending aspiration of human civilization.” Even if it's not to our satisfaction, Nigerians before us have played their part in getting us here. It is our turn to take it further.

title: How do we build Technology for the Informal Sector & Poorly Educated in Nigeria?
writing:
I was among a group of factory workers when I suddenly asked myself, "How do we build useful technology for this demographic?" By demographic, I meant unskilled laborers that are not adequately educated and might have difficulty using a smartphone. How do we build useful technology for such an illiterate group?

The reason this question is important is that, according to different sources, 80 to 90% of employed Nigerians work in the informal sector. This is astonishingly high, but it also indicates the informal sector is where technology will have the most profound and pervasive impact. It's also safe to assume from these statistics that Nigeria's literacy level is very low.

Again, how do we build technology for such a group? I think this is a situation peculiar to Nigeria and Africa at large.

This led to another question: "What is the state of technology adoption in Nigeria?" After some brainstorming, I realized the most adopted technology is the smartphone, and then other forms of technology—primarily software—flow from it in the form of mobile apps. This is fair considering the ubiquity of smartphones. However, the sad part is: (1) the smartphones are the only technology widely adopted across Nigeria, and (2) even on our smartphones, the most used mobile apps are the ones financially oriented. Beyond finance, we mostly use communication apps like WhatsApp, but I can't think of locally-built apps addressing other critical aspects of Nigerian life—transportation, healthcare, education, agriculture—at any meaningful scale. These sectors remain largely untouched by Nigerian-built technology.

I hate to state the obvious, but technology isn't restricted to smartphones and mobile apps. Technology can be in our transportation/energy, government and military, banking, education, and hospitals. Building hardware and software technology in these areas is how we can offer technological services to the informal sector and poorly educated.

A question I asked myself while brainstorming is, "Do we need literacy to be widespread for technological adoption to be high?" No. I don't believe so. I came to the conclusion that the informal sector and poorly educated are not the problem. Rather, it's the formally educated population that is to blame for not having the know-how to build technologies. How can we expect adoption of technologies we can't even build?

What has become clear to me from this writing is that we do not need to re-organize and educate our informal sector and poorly educated population before they can use technology. Proof of this is the smartphones, mobile apps, and POS machines that are already in use by these people. Instead, what we need is a more capable formally educated population that can build technology keeping in mind the class of people they're building for. This is what we're doing with WinehouseLabs.

It goes without saying that a high literate population will be nice to have. But I do not think the literacy level is a barrier to technological adoption. I believe a more literate population will inevitably follow a nation as it prospers.

I will spend more time with people in the informal sector, pay attention to their activities, and see what we can build to make their lives better. I think the best place to start, though, is to improve our competence in software. After that, we get into hardware to build tangible things for different aspects of the Nigerian life: marketplaces, transports, schools, hospitals, etcetera.

title: Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller, Sr
writing:
## On John D. Rockefeller Sr.
If I could ask Rockefeller a question, it would be: “How did you reconcile being a ruthless businessman with also being a devout Christian?” Rockefeller was a ruthless businessman, and I have no doubts he was guilty of the alleged bribery and corruption he was accused of that made Standard Oil the great company it became.

I am more interested in his business philosophy and business practices; his preference for cooperation over competition, and his thinking in managing Standard Oil.

A misconception some of his contemporaries had of him was that he was unsophisticated and didn’t have any ideology. This is a grave mistake. I consider Rockefeller a profound thinker and someone that stood for something other than just making money. You get glimpses of his ideology via his constant argument to bring order to the chaotic oil industry by cooperation instead of competition, his adoption of new technologies—like the pipeline and research scientists—to maintain Standard Oil’s monopoly, his vast vertical integration operation, and his principle on helping people without weakening their moral backbone.

If Father Abraham is considered the patriarch of Abrahamic religions, I consider Rockefeller the father of capitalism, where every modern capitalist practice originated from.

## On Cooperation vs. Competition
A recurring argument in the book is whether cooperation (meaning monopoly) is better than competition. My stance is that cooperation is good and justified as long as it continues to innovate. I believe a monopoly becomes a liability to the world the moment it stops building new things, thereby holding back progress. The world is filled with examples of monopolies that have died after failing to keep up with innovation. Some examples are Nokia, BlackBerry, and IBM.

A good monopoly that currently exists is Google. Google is a behemoth that has data on almost every human on the planet. But I consider its monopoly justified because it continues to innovate, thereby giving the world more progress with Google DeepMind, Waymo, Isomorphic Labs, and many more research projects the public most likely don’t even know about.

So, like Peter Thiel said, and like Rockefeller observed, “competition is for losers.” Competition is a cut-throat distraction that takes your focus away from building new things because you are constantly fighting for survival.

Monopoly, on the other hand, is justified as long as it continues to move the world forward. The moment it stops, it should be killed.

## On Standard Oil
One important aspect of Standard Oil’s success was the existence of a financial system that was accessible and capable of providing Rockefeller the needed capital whenever he needed it. It is not an exaggeration to say if these banks never existed or were inaccessible for loans like Nigerian banks are, then there would have been no Standard Oil.

This lesson reinforces my belief that Nigeria needs a robust and accessible financial system and center that can help fund the entrepreneurial ambitions of credible and worthy Nigerians.

Another observation I had is the infancy of the American legislative system during the rise and even domination of Standard Oil. This is very similar to the current state of Nigeria’s legislative system.

This situation is a double-edged sword because while it provides a lot of opportunities for entrepreneurs to abuse the law so as to accelerate their progress like Standard Oil did, it also puts the country and citizens in a perilous state where, if the legislatures do not catch up, then the whole country risks being at the mercy of one great, gigantic company.

I think a situation like this is unavoidable. What is important is that as these two parallel lines (that is, entrepreneurship and the legislature) continue to advance, the legislature should find a balance between regulating entrepreneurship and avoiding stifling innovation.

The danger an infant legislature poses is evident in the anticompetitive practices used by Standard Oil to become a monopoly. This included bribery, dominating and abusing the supply chain, predatory pricing, and even industrial espionage. While I admire Rockefeller greatly and believe entrepreneurship is a dog-eat-dog world, I have to admit these are anticompetitive practices taken to a whole new level.

The unfair things that Standard Oil did to dominate the oil industry shouldn’t blind us from the fact that the company was also filled with A-players that made the company's success possible. This is a fact acknowledged even by the company’s fiercest critic, Ida Tarbell, when she said, “there was not a lazy bone in the organization, not an incompetent hand, nor a stupid head.”

There is a lesson here, and it’s that even if you have an advantage to win but you have an incompetent team, you will lose.

## On Rockefeller Philanthropy
Rockefeller’s philanthropic endeavors have a very important lesson for not just philanthropies but also nation-building, and it’s this: how do we help people without weakening their moral backbone?

This reminds me of a lesson from Benjamin Franklin on avoiding making social welfare so comfortable for the poor that they give up the willingness to be hardworking, responsible citizens. Like he said, “…the best way of doing good to the poor is not making them easy in poverty, but leading or driving them out of it.”

The Rockefeller Foundation’s principle in helping was on “finding the underpinnings of poverty” then getting rid of them. They accomplished this by building schools and universities to increase literacy, helping people acquire vocational skills, and succeeding in overcoming health-related challenges to make citizens healthier and more active.

This is how I believe philanthropy and social welfare should be executed to ensure sustainability.

Continue to rest in peace, John D. Rockefeller Sr.

title: Why I Am Studying Computer Science
writing:
When I bought my laptop, the first skills I learnt were Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator, and After Effects. My intention was to use these skills to build a business that would have a widespread impact—a business with ubiquitous services. But then I realized they weren’t tech skills. They were really just design skills. I don’t regret the time I spent learning them, though, because they come in handy when building things.

Then I discovered programming—writing code. I realized programming skills are what I need if I’m going to build a high-impact business like, say, Google. The leverage is massive, and the barrier to entry is almost zero. So, I started learning how to program.

The deeper I got into programming and as I watched interviews of different software engineers using terms I wasn’t familiar with, the more convinced I was that some of these people had a kind of knowledge that went beyond just writing code. It was computer science.

I realized there are levels to being a software engineer. You can be someone who just knows how to write code and build things, or you can be a god-like engineer who not only writes code but also has a deep understanding of how computers work.

The more I thought about this, the more I saw how important computer science is to the world we live in today. Computers of all kinds are becoming more and more integrated into human life—our phones, AI, laptops, and so on. If I’m going to be one of the people building things with real impact, then I need to study computer science.

Computer science is the backbone of the innovations shaping our era. It’s the gateway to jobs that build the future. And if I’m going to be part of building that future, I need to study computer science.

title: Is Intelligence Determined by Genetics or One's Environment?
writing:
The reason this question is important is to determine if we Nigerians are capable of replicating the technological and scientific progress achieved by developed countries like the US and China, or if we’ve just been condemned by God to be less intelligent people. Or worse, stupid.

I think the best place to start is by questioning popular assumptions we have of people from other countries when it comes to talent. Like, do Americans just happen to be better than the rest of the world at computers and software? Is it true Asians have an inherent quality that makes them better than the rest of us at math? Were the Germans handpicked by God to be the best in engineering and the automotive industry? Is there something about the Jews that makes them good at physics?

Your answer to these questions will determine if you think genes dictate intelligence, or if intelligence is just something to be nurtured.

Research says it's a mixture of both, but my stance is that intelligence is something to be nurtured and willed into existence with a great deal of stubbornness. The individual—or people—need to insist that, come rain or sunshine, the knowledge in whatever field shall be attained, and it must. I agree biology will play its role in one's cognitive abilities, but I insist the major determinant is the individual and his environment.

There is nothing special about the Americans, Chinese, or Germans that makes them more intelligent than a Nigerian, and it is this mindset that will enable us to achieve technological and scientific progress ourselves.

title: Benjamin Franklin by Walter Isaacson
writing:
I don’t know what to make of Benjamin Franklin, to be honest. The man is hard to fit into a box. He’s slippery, and even in death it feels like he’s still playing tricks on you. I’m not the only one struggling with this. Even his contemporaries and people generations after alternate between reverence and resentment towards him.

My anger at him stems from how he treated his family. Normally, you’d expect more love and compassion for one’s immediate family than for outsiders. His case was different. He showered friends—especially women—with more attention and affection than he gave his own children and wife. He was absent at both of his children's weddings and, worse, spent sixteen years away from his wife without seeing her till she died lonely.

A lot of great men I’ve read about fall decisively into either of 2 categories; the good or the bad side. In his case, he is always alternating between the 2 depending on the trend and whatever you might have read on him. In my book, though, he is on the good side of history.

### What Made Him Great?

Benjamin Franklin is the only Founding Father of America I’ve read a book on so far, but I’d still consider him my favorite even before reading about the others. He comes across as simple and funny—the kind of old man a young person would love to sit with and talk to. That charm is evident in how many family and friends wanted to spend time with him in his old age, which is rare. I hope to have that when I’m old.

What earned him a seat among history’s greats was his **wisdom**. From his days as a print apprentice to his service as colonial delegate and ambassador, he carried a rare, sage-like wisdom.

Of course, he was intelligent—his business and scientific achievements prove that. But wisdom played a bigger role in his accomplishments and, most importantly, in helping America win its war with Britain.

There’s a distinction between **intelligence** and **wisdom**. Intelligence is more overt and useful in getting things done—math, science, programming, and so on. Wisdom is more subtle, a level higher. You can’t be wise without intelligence, but you can be intelligent without having wisdom.

For example, **John Adams** was intelligent but not wise. Wisdom is knowing what to say and when to say it, being strategic, manipulative when necessary, and playing down your own brilliance. Franklin did all that to perfection.

### Benjamin Franklin and American Values

The values he lived by became the foundation of “the American Dream.” He believed in egalitarianism, industriousness, scientific discovery, technological progress, shameless ambition for upward mobility, practicality, community-driven initiatives, and patriotism. That entire philosophy is what “the American Dream” stands for.

The idea that regardless of your social status, with hard work you can rise to the top—and once you do, you owe it to your country to give back—is exactly what America became. Hardworking citizens becoming billionaires, then reinvesting their fortunes in the nation through philanthropy. This cycle helped make America the superpower it is today.

That’s the biggest lesson I took from the book: **if Nigeria is going to achieve long-term, sustainable progress, we must lay down better values.**

### Postscript

I don’t think anyone deserves the title “Founding Father of America” more than Benjamin Franklin. He is the only man to have his signature on all four documents that created the country:

1. The Declaration of Independence
2. The treaty with France
3. The peace accord with Britain
4. The Constitution

How can anyone beat that? I’m sure he’d smirk reading this.

*Rest in peace, Benjamin Franklin.*

title: Leonardo Da Vinci
writing:
The reason I bought this book is because I believe art is very important. I consider myself first and foremost an entrepreneur, but if in the process of building things we neglect the importance of art, then we’ll end up building a country looking like the Soviet Union.

My favorite lesson from the book was learning about the Renaissance era. It felt like a magical time when humans realized how much they’re capable of and then started creating cool things. It’s a shame this spirit no longer exists anywhere in the world. 

The most remarkable thing about the Renaissance is the depth the people went to acquire knowledge and then applying it to works like architecture, sculpting, and painting. An example is Leonardo Da Vinci dissecting human bodies just so he could know what muscles do what, so he could then use the knowledge to influence his painting. Another example is the attempt to show how the inner emotions of humans in paintings manifest in their outward gestures. These are knowledge that are not very important to get the work done, but they’re also the reason the paintings from that era—over 500 years ago—remain masterpieces till this day.

There is something about the Renaissance that feels magical and that the current generation might never be capable of replicating. Evidence of this is the stark difference between the art created then versus now. Examples are the Mona Lisa created by Leonardo Da Vinci, the Sistine Chapel and sculpture of David by Michelangelo, The Prince by Machiavelli, Dante’s Inferno, and the Dome of Florence by Filippo Brunelleschi.

We might have built impressive things in the modern age, but none of our art equals what came out of the Renaissance.

## On Learning

The other lesson I found very valuable was on how the people of the Renaissance approached learning. I am constantly learning, so their suggestions were very valuable to me.

My favorite suggestion was from Roger Bacon. He emphasized a cycle: that observations should lead to a hypothesis, which should then be tested by precise experiments, which would then be used to refine the original hypothesis.

Another valuable suggestion was from Leonardo, who suggested learning from experience, experimentation, and analogy. An advice from him says, “If you wish to have a sound knowledge of the form of objects, begin with details of them, and do not go to the second step until you have the first well fixed in memory.”

I consider these advice very important and intend to apply them going forward.

## On Leonardo Da Vinci

I have no doubt Leonardo Da Vinci was a genius, but he also had qualities that held him back from being as great as he could have been. Those qualities are lack of focus and procrastination.

He was widely acknowledged as a genius among his contemporaries, but he could have been much more if he had just focused and finished his projects.

His disappointment in himself is evident from the envy he felt towards other artists that were regularly receiving commissions from patrons, while he accumulated a reputation as someone that never completed his work. It is debated that on his deathbed he apologized to “God and man for leaving so much undone.”

There is so much to learn from the genius, but for anyone that aspires to build great things, the habit of procrastination and lack of focus must be killed. At the end, the world will judge us by our results and not the numerous unfinished projects we have lying around.

Make sure you always see things to the end, Wariz.

title: What companies like Cowrywise and Chowdeck tell us about the people that will build Nigeria
writing:
There is something that hasn’t been getting the attention it deserves, and it’s the remarkable team of young people working in companies like Cowrywise, Chowdeck, and PiggyVest. **Emphasis on “young people”.** 

The value of these young people comes in the form of design, programming, and marketing, and their effectiveness is evident in the popularity of these companies’ products and designs. It’s proof that young people can solve problems in Nigeria by each bringing their unique abilities to the table. 

The only admonition I have is that these talents should also be diverted into solving other painful and important problems in sectors like **transportation, education, healthcare, and security.** This is the only way Nigeria will see holistic progress on all fronts; our forces need to focus on tackling and solving the different problems plaguing the country. 

**Talent exist. Direction is what’s left.**

title: Democracy doesn’t work in Nigeria. I choose a cabal
writing:
There is a saying by Lee Kuan Yew: ***"leadership has to be exercised in the context of the society it is in."*** This means that before we impose a system of government on a people, we should consider their nuances. We've failed to do this in Nigeria.

I am not against democracy. In fact, I believe a democratic system is the best system of government. The problem, however, is that democracies only thrive in countries with a large number of talented citizens capable of upholding democratic institutions. Nigeria doesn't have this.

The reason is that I believe Nigeria has a talent problem, and to ascertain the quality of our people, we should look at the deplorable state of every sector in our country: healthcare, banking, policing, teaching, and most importantly, government. No sector works as it should.

I am not saying Nigeria completely lacks quality and talented citizens. What I mean is that the unqualified outnumber the qualified by a great deal. For this reason, I'd suggest a system where the qualified minority rules the majority. A cabal.

The primary principle in democracy is egalitarianism — the belief that everyone is equal and should therefore be treated equally. This includes having the right to vote and be voted for. While this is noble, it doesn't mean it's right. In a country like Nigeria, where thugs and illiterates participate in the electoral process that dictates the next four to eight years of our lives, this democratic principle has a negative effect.

There is something called *"the madness of crowds,"* where individuals in a large group lose their senses, causing them to make irrational decisions. I believe Nigeria has been misled by the madness of the crowd. We should take control.

## A cabal

The word "cabal" is often seen as bad because it insinuates secrecy, manipulation, and bad intent by a small group of people. While these descriptions of a cabal are correct, the part I disagree with is "bad intent." Our cabal should be secretive and manipulate political and economic events behind the scenes, but its intent must be a positive one — to fix Nigeria.

My primary argument for the establishment of this cabal is to free it from the shackles of democratic principles like egalitarianism and checks and balances, so as to have a political force capable of making the tough decisions required to fix the country and move fast.

Despite how controversial this writing is, I don't believe the idea I am proposing is new. In fact, I believe a cabal-like state is what is being practiced in two countries I admire — Singapore and China — but in different forms.

On the surface, Singapore appears democratic and does uphold democratic values like egalitarianism and inclusivity, but the reverse is also true: it is being run by a tight group of people who share the same values and allow the continuation of long-term plans that won't be disrupted by an opposition. The People's Action Party (PAP) of Singapore has been in power since 1959, and the gap between it and its opposition is not significant enough to pose a threat to the party's continuity.

Then there is China. I agree that China is an authoritarian communist regime, but it has a lot of similarities with what I am proposing. China is ruled by the Communist Party of China (CPC), but within that party, power is concentrated in a small elite circle with Xi Jinping as its head. A cabal.

The examples I've drawn from these two countries illustrate unique advantages that are difficult to find in a democracy — namely long-term planning and execution, because power is concentrated in the hands of a group that shares the same values, consistency, and, most importantly, minority rule.

We've allowed unqualified people to vote and rule Nigeria for too long. We've allowed them to run our local, state, and federal offices, and we've appointed them into ministries and police ranks. Majority rule doesn't work. Let's try something else — **a cabal.**

When its time for implementation we'll talk about how to keep the cabal in check.

title: I believe we live in a magical world. Unfortunately, very few people know this
writing:
200 years from now, when everyone reading this is dead, there will be books about people like Elon Musk, Tinubu, Putin, and Donald Trump. There will be books about events that happened in our lifetime—events like the COVID-19 pandemic and the arrival of artificial intelligence. There will be books about wars we’re experiencing, like the Russia-Ukraine war, the Israel-Palestine conflict, and the US-Iran war. There will be books about great artists existing at the same time as us—artists like Kanye West and K1 De Ultimate.

This is the same way books exist on crazy events that happened long before we were born—events like WWI and WWII, the dropping of the atomic bomb, the Industrial and Digital Revolutions, and the US-Vietnam war. The same way books also exist on great people who lived before us—people like Einstein, Leonardo da Vinci, Lee Kuan Yew, Masaru Ibuka, Akio Morita, and many others.

The point I’m trying to make is that our actions matter and we can do amazing things before it’s inevitably our time to leave. The important question to now ask is: **do you want to participate?**

title: Source Code by Bill Gates
writing:
The first impression I had when I bought this book was that it would be another biography written to whitewash the person's image. But I was wrong. Bill Gates was very honest in this book, at least to a satisfactory degree.

When it comes to Bill Gates, especially in his old age, there are a lot of conspiracy theories. Some claim he is part of a so-called "global elite" that wants to take over the world by creating a "New World Order" and intentionally releasing COVID-19 to cause millions of deaths and make billions of dollars. To be honest, I believe some of these conspiracy theories. But even if they're 100% true, I think it would be absurd to expect him to reveal such information. This is why I say I am satisfied with the degree of honesty in the book.

In the book, he wrote about his insecurities, his luck, and his arrogance. He also discussed his bad attitudes towards his parents and his alpha-male domination while building Microsoft with Paul Allen. If we are expecting a book on Bill Gates written by the man himself, then this level of truthfulness is acceptable. It is better than other biographies where the writer paints themselves as a saint all through.

Despite the huge difference in the worlds we were both born into, I related a lot to the book; the parts about reading, about working long hours, going all-in on Microsoft, and the obsession and drive to make his company successful. These are the hardcore experiences every true entrepreneur wants to have before they grow old and reflect on their life.

I think the most important gift the book gave me is the different timelines it put me in: one where he is young like myself with so much time on his hands to build something, and the other where I know Bill is 69 years old and done with his entrepreneurial journey. It made me realize I am currently in the 1st timeline (young Bill) and, if I live long enough, will also end up in the 2nd. This made me restless and impatient to work harder and be more serious before I get to that 2nd timeline.

To my fellow "conspiracy theorists" who will judge the book a failure because he didn't write about his involvement in being part of the "global elite," I think that's something absurd to expect. My question is: if you were in his shoes, would you admit to being part of such a group?

But maybe I am getting ahead of myself. Maybe Bill will shock us by writing about or mentioning the global elite in the other parts of his biography. Cheers till then.

title: The war against counterfeit medicine by Dora Nkem Akunyili
writing:
When you go on social media and you see Nigerians complain about Nigeria and her citizens, you’d think the people from the country are the worst set of humans to ever exist. You might consume so much anti-Nigerian content that it will leave you believing Nigerians are inherently evil, stupid, and incompetent.

This book tells a different story. It shows that with the right leadership and environment, Nigerians are competent and good-hearted people.

When reading the book, it’s easy to get carried away with the technical things Prof. Akunyili achieved as Director General of NAFDAC. First, she revitalized the dead agency through reorganization and the building of standard NAFDAC offices and laboratories. Then, she improved the welfare of NAFDAC employees with better remuneration, and improved their capabilities via local and international training. These two factors created an effective NAFDAC administration that came up with brilliant ideas to drastically reduce the number of fake medicines and food substances in circulation.

Now, her influence didn’t end in NAFDAC offices. She was also able to enlist the support of the Nigerian press to create awareness, get the Nigerian public—both literate and non-literate—to take part in the fight against counterfeit medicines, and get support from state governments and government agencies to curb the spread of fake medicines. Everything coalesced in helping her achieve her goal.

In the book, she presents statistics to show how much NAFDAC achieved under her leadership. While the results are great, I don’t consider them her greatest achievement because I saw something more profound, and that is the unification of the Nigerian people in the pursuit of a single cause to make something work. This is her greatest achievement in my opinion.

She proved Nigerians are good-hearted, competent people, and that with the right leadership, environment, and incentives, we can do great things.

 ### You can make Nigerians do great things.

title: The Innovators Dilemma by Prof. Clayton Christensen
writing:
My aim with this writing is not to review *The Innovator's Dilemma* by Prof. Christensen. Instead, my goal is to draw lessons from the book to prove we don't need cutting-edge technologies before we can solve problems in Nigeria and build viable businesses. We just need to rethink our approach to solving problems.

What *The Innovator's Dilemma* is ultimately about is how successful businesses can lose their market dominance even when they make the right decisions. The "right decisions" here means following conventional management advice like listening to your customers and continuously improving your product.

He adds that these conventional management decisions are what initially lead to businesses being successful and dominant. However, when a disruptive technology comes along, the business needs to rethink the decisions it follows. This will be difficult because of forces that will make it nearly impossible to continue to dominate the market with the arrival of the disruptive technology.

He mentions one solution to this dilemma is to establish a new and independent business outside the main business that will make commercializing the disruptive technology its primary focus.

---

### Lessons for Nigeria
I think the most valuable lessons in this book are the concepts that put successful businesses at a disadvantage when it comes to maintaining their dominance. If we can internalize these concepts, we can then identify opportunities in the Nigerian market. The next thing should be to build disruptive technologies to provide better solutions.

### What does Disruptive Technologies mean?
Two concepts that are important in the book are **"sustaining innovations"** and **"disruptive innovations."** We can flip them to sustaining products and disruptive products for easier understanding.

What they mean is:

* **(i) Sustaining products** are products that businesses continuously improve to give their customers better experiences so as to stay competitive in the market. An example is ATM machines introduced by banks to enable customer withdrawal from any branch.
* **(ii) Disruptive products**, on the other hand, are products—often introduced by new entrants into the market—that offer simpler, cheaper, or more convenient experiences than existing products in the market. An example is the introduction of POS machines that made transfer and withdrawal of funds more convenient than ATM machines. This led to banks losing revenue from ATM machines.

Disruptive products eventually overthrow sustaining products in the market, causing the new entrants to dominate the market formerly dominated by successful businesses.

The good news is that disruptive products don't require groundbreaking technological advancement that might not be accessible to Nigerians. Disruptive products can be something as simple as offering the market a service or product in a better way. 

> As Prof. Christensen put it, "disruptive technologies don't need to involve new technologies; rather, they consist of components built around proven technologies put together in a novel product architecture that offers the customer a set of attributes never before accessible."

### Why should we build Disruptive Products?
The importance of building disruptive products is numerous. There is the economic aspect that makes our country more productive and prosperous, the development aspect that improves the quality of life of our people, and there is also the advantage of overthrowing businesses that aren't serving the Nigerian population honestly and competently.

I believe if we pursue this goal of finding better solutions and businesses for problems, then these advantages will coalesce into making Nigeria a developed country.

### Do we even have the Capabilities to Create Disruptive Products?
If it's building and using sophisticated technologies like AI, robotics, automation, microprocessors, etc., then the honest answer is no. But as we've seen, creating disruptive products doesn't necessarily require these groundbreaking sophisticated technologies that are out of our reach.

What we need is to build our disruptive products around proven technologies and skills that we can access, then we continue to move up from there. An example is **software engineering**.

Something important to add is that we should never consider these sophisticated technologies as things that will forever be out of Nigeria's reach. China and the USA did not start out as countries flourishing with these technologies. This proves technological prowess is a capability that can be acquired. And we will.

title: The Hundred Years’ War on Palestine by Rashid Khalidi
writing:
The most important lesson I learnt from reading this book is how much of our destiny is tied to the decisions of our leaders—if our leaders consistently make bad decisions, then such decisions are bound to play a significant role in making us unfortunate.

There are many factors to blame for the unfortunate events happening to the Palestinians, but what takes the cake is the incessant incompetence of the Palestinian and Arab leaders. While the leaders of Israel were united and committed to Zionism, the Palestinian and Arab leaders were naïve and selfish, preferring to sacrifice their people’s welfare in exchange for validation from countries like the USA and Britain.

Examples of this bad leadership are the lack of support and betrayal from Arab leaders towards the Palestinians despite belonging to the same ethnicity, and the constant infighting and internal conflict among Palestinians instead of focusing on their common enemy—Israel.

After blaming the Palestinian leaders for the misfortune of their people, it is also important to be honest about the unfair advantage Israel enjoyed from superpowers like Britain and the USA. Israel enjoyed a lot of political, military, and financial support from these two countries, which helped expel Palestinians from their land. This, however, does not absolve Palestinian leaders of their incompetence.

> As Elon Musk said, only “conspicuous acts of kindness” from Israel towards the Palestinians will end this war. This, however, is unlikely to happen considering it does not conform to Zionism.

title: Like the ascent of the internet in the 1990s, I predict AI will create a new set of billionaires
writing:
I have a prediction, and it's that the AI era we're currently witnessing will create a new set of billionaires like the internet did in the 1990s and early 2000s.

The internet revolution started in the mid-1990s, and from it, billion-dollar companies were birthed. Some of these companies are PayPal, Google, Amazon, Facebook, YouTube, and many others. The founders of these companies remain billionaires to this day. Men like Elon Musk and Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, Bill Gates, and Jeff Bezos.

While a lot of these men are still active and even dominant in the tech scene today, I predict that in the coming years, the world will see a new set of billionaires whose wealth will primarily come from the ascent of AI. Just like Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos leveraged the internet, this new set of billionaires will leverage AI.

Now, a common misconception I observe when listening to people talk about AI is how the money to be made is concentrated at the complicated technological skills and knowledge required to build AI. You hear things like "NVIDIA," "infrastructure," "chips," and so on. They talk about the resources and skills that go into building AI, neglecting the superpowers the AI bot itself will give ordinary people who don't possess these technical skills — at least not yet.

While these people are right — about selling shovels in a gold rush, like Jensen Huang — about the money to be made from building AI, my prediction is that the majority of the next set of billionaires will come from ordinary, ambitious people leveraging AI chatbots and other forms AI comes in to build companies. I place my bet here.

Now, the question that has kept me busy is: what shape or form will these new companies take? To be honest, I don't know, and I'm confident no one else does. We'll all have to constantly try new things with this new technology, then look back 20 years to see what worked and what didn't. But if I were to guess, I would say these new companies will involve driverless cars, factory robots, software, intelligence, and AI-powered weapons.

The last thing I will add is that this is a huge opportunity for Africans. The African builders that leverage this technology will shape not just their respective countries, but the continent.

title: Why I love Bola Ahmed Tinubu
writing:
I want to begin this writing by saying my intention here is not to vouch for BAT's integrity or debate if he stole public funds or not. I believe every great man is flawed, and that humanity has to take the good with the bad. My intention is to talk about the qualities that I believe make BAT the greatest politician to come out of this country.

I am not oblivious to the fact that the country is currently hard on people; the economy is difficult and insecurity is prevalent. So, a writing like this may feel out of place. If this writing is however read with an open mind, then I believe the reader will be more objective about BAT's accomplishments.

The title of this writing is already bold but I have a bolder statement, and it's that in the history of Nigeria's politics, I believe BAT is the greatest politician. I have three factors to prove this and they are Lagos, his successors, and his ideology.

## Lagos

There is no doubt that Lagos is the most successful state in the country. Without the economic metrics and data visualization, the state's  success is evident to the deaf and blind, and this is why everyone flocks there.

While everyone is aware of this, the majority assume Lagos' prosperity happened naturally, or some will say it happened because it was formerly the capital of Nigeria. But nowhere in the world does something happen without someone engineering it.

When Tinubu became governor of Lagos in 1999, there was really no difference between Lagos and the other states. Lagos was like every other state; poor and dependent on the federal government. There were many decisions BAT made as governor of Lagos, but the one that is primarily responsible for Lagos' prosperity–up till this day–was his decision to make Lagos economically independent of the federal government. He did this by radically improving the state's tax system; this decision is the reason Lagos generated 1.7 trillion naira in IGR in 2025, which now funds state infrastructures and expenses.

The success of this single decision is more outstanding when you realize Lagos consistently generates more IGR than thirty other Nigerian states combined. While many states still depend on federal allocation (FAAC) to meet their expenses, Lagos's IGR accounts for 70% of its revenue, meaning it can fully function without the FAAC allocation.

Improving the tax system is just one piece of the puzzle. The ripple effect of this decision has also led to many other actions like encouraging entrepreneurship and attracting foreign investments that all come together to make Lagos what it is. At the end of the day, what's the point of an effective tax system if there are no increased economic activities?

Is Lagos rough and unhealthy? Yes. But is it more successful and prosperous? Also yes. Two things can be true.

## His Successors

Dr. Kadri Hamzat, who as of this writing is currently the deputy governor of Lagos State, narrated a  visit to Singapore with then governor Babatunde Raji Fashola where they met Lee Kuan Yew. The first thing Lee Kuan Yew had asked them was, "Do you have a succession plan?"

The reason this question is so important is because no matter how hard you work and how successful you are at building something, what determines the sustainability of what you've built is a good succession plan to make sure the people that come after you don't screw things up. This BAT succeeded in.

BAT did two things to ensure his successors are competent, worthy people; first was his establishment of the Governance Advisory Council (GAC), and second is the quality of people he nurtured to take over from him.

The GAC is often misunderstood as a cabal that forces a governor on Lagosians, but that is not true. The GAC exists simply for the sake of stability. After the GAC picks a candidate for the APC party, Lagosians still have the freedom to vote against that person at the ballot boxes. The foresight BAT had in creating the GAC was to prevent political squabbles that hinder progress and give way to incompetent people becoming governor. Proof of this is the condition of the governors' offices in other states; there are no continuity plans and no synergy. Just one person coming into office after another.

The effectiveness of the GAC is evident in the people that have become governors after BAT; Fashola, Ambode, Sanwo-Olu, and most likely Dr. Hamzat. The worst performer on this list was Ambode, and even he can be considered better than most governors from other states. We can say anything we want about each of these Lagos governors, but one thing we can't say about them is that they did not work and bring something new to Lagos.

## His Ideology

My definition of an ideology or mantra is an idea or way of life you believe in and pursue with all your might. Examples are whether you're a capitalist, communist, libertarian, conservative, progressive, and so on.

In Nigeria, politicians rarely have an ideology. I don't think I've ever read of a Nigerian politician that articulated an idea or way of life he or she believes in. This is why they defect from one party to another with no idea what they're doing (this excludes men like Obafemi Awolowo and Nnamdi Azikiwe that fought for Nigeria's independence).

Tinubu's mantra and ideology is something he calls "Renewed Hope". The first public utterance of this phrase was in 1999 when he was governor and addressing the state. That was 27 years ago. How many Nigerian politicians can you think of that have had an ideology going that far back? Literally none exist.

---

Now you might ask what these 3 points will do in fixing Nigeria. And my answer to that is BAT can't fix Nigeria because Nigeria's problem is generational. I don't mean this in a superstitious way but literally. For Nigeria to work, each generation must be committed to making it work. So if anyone expects BAT to fix Nigeria in under eight years, then that tells us a lot about the person.

My intention with this writing is to ask that when debating BAT and thinking of a new leader, we should consider these three metrics; does he or she have tangible results of his or her competence, who are the person's successors or protégés, and do they believe in anything? Do they stand for something?

If you think I'm wrong in saying BAT is the greatest politician to come out of this country, then I challenge you to name a worthy competitor.

title: American Prometheus
writing:
## On J. Robert Oppenheimer

Oppie was a remarkably smart man. An intelligent man. In a world where there are different kinds of intelligence, I'd pick to have his; the ability to talk physics, politics, philosophy, and a range of other topics is the kind of intelligence I admire.

As for his communist ties that led to his 1954 humiliation, I don't know what to make of it. I don't think he did anything wrong socializing with communists. Rather, I think he was just a victim of the unfortunate McCarthyite hysteria that gripped America at the time. Like he said "It was as if a building was falling and I was just there".

The only place I fault him was not listening to Einstein's advice to just resign from the AEC. Why didn't he do that? I guess his vanity got the best of him.

## The 1954 security hearing

I've never thought of "legacy" as something important. Or as something that matters. But after reading this book I think it does matter. I don't care what anyone thinks of me. But what people think and say about us after we're dead matters. Because that is our legacy. That is all we leave behind. That is what will be passed from one generation to the next.

To everyone, it might seem like Lewis Strauss defeated Oppenheimer with the 1954 hearing—and he did—but in the process he totally ruined his legacy. His reputation. A Google search of his name and the first thing that comes up is his obsession and insanity to destroy Oppenheimer. For a man with such a delicate skin and ambition, I bet he would be crying in his grave knowing that's how he is remembered. That this is his legacy.

## On Nuclear weapons

I believe a time will come when nuclear weapons will actually be used. Where there would be a nuclear war. When this will happen I don't know. Why do I think it will happen? Because nuclear weapons exist. My theory is simple; the inevitability of a nuclear war exists because nuclear weapons exist.

I don't know the circumstances or the degree or intensity of hostility that will precipitate this horrible war. I am even trembling as I type this prediction. But when it does happen, all we can do is to try to survive. It's not like we've not been suffering up to that point. Like Nietzsche said, "to live is to suffer. To survive is to find some meaning in the suffering".

Till then.

title: Why we must study European, American, and Chinese civilization
writing:
Why we must study European, American, and Chinese civilization

Nigeria is a very young country, so there's no shame in admitting there is a lot we don't know regarding the political and economic theories that shape nations. And I would argue that an absence of these theories can be blamed for our country not working.

The foremost political theory that we're aware of is the idea of democracy, but we've only adopted this due to its prevalence in the 21st century — not because it is what we consider ideal and compatible with our way of life. Considering our uniqueness, we should also have theories in economics, social structures, education, etc. that serve as an anchor when making policies for each sector.

I should also add that I'm not asking us to reinvent the wheel. Great minds like Aristotle, Adam Smith, and Nietzsche already have brilliant ideas that can be adopted or tweaked to conform to our peculiarities.

For example, among other theories, the Chinese also have Confucianism, which emphasizes the importance of family and meritocracy; the Americans have an almost fanatical belief in the concept of freedom; different countries either adopt Adam Smith's capitalism or Karl Marx's communism; then there's also Thomas Hobbes' Social Contract, David Hume's political discourses, Montesquieu's separation of powers, and many more.

These are political and economic theories from countries whose civilization is far more advanced than ours — proof that they work. We don't — and should not — adopt them as a whole, but tweak them to fit our context.

The earlier we can consider these theories, the earlier we can have ideas to serve as an anchor when shaping Nigeria.

title: Why I Love Peter Thiel
writing:
I believe Peter Thiel is a very important figure in a world that is gradually seeing a decline of ambitious people and communities. In a time like this, we need extremely smart people like him to remind us of the important things we should be working on.

Thiel has many brilliant ideas, a lot of which I subscribe to. There is: competition is for losers, zero to one vs one to N, definite optimism, vertical vs horizontal progress, and the idea of "developed vs developing world." The last one is the most important because it encapsulates the other ideas.

**"Developed vs Developing World"**

What Thiel is arguing here is that using language like "developed" and "developing" world is wrong because it suggests the former is fully developed — therefore there is nothing left to build — and the latter simply has to catch up by copying the developed world. Note that "world" here means country.

The reason this argument is so important is because it points to a deeper problem in the West, and that is that people there have stopped innovating. Worse — and this is a bigger fear of Thiel's — there is a decline across the US and Europe when it comes to ambition. He believes that compared to the past, the current generation of Americans and Europeans are poorly ambitious as a people.

**Applying Thiel's Ideas to Nigeria**

Putting the debate on developed vs developing world aside, there are some other brilliant ideas from him that we can apply to building Nigeria. The first, and my favourite, is "definite optimism." This simply means believing that the future will be better if you plan and work for it. This view is very important because I don't think Nigeria has ever had a leader with a definite vision of how he wants the country's future to look.

Thiel argues that if you want the future to be better, you have to work towards making it happen. In a country like Nigeria that is disorganised, this is a very important idea to adopt.

Another important Thiel idea is "competition is for losers." What he means is that as an entrepreneur, you should build companies that no one else is building. Solve problems that no one else is attempting to solve. Leave competitive businesses like opening a restaurant to others while you focus on building a monopoly.

I believe this is also an important idea we should adopt in Nigeria. A lot of businesses that don't move the country forward in any significant way are over-saturated — while there are also very important problems we could be solving to make the country better.

I think we should listen more to Peter Thiel.
